name: Fire Stealing Bird
description: In the Polynesian origin-of-fire cycle the keeper of fire is a little bird, most famously the ʻalae ʻula (Hawaiian mudhen), whose flock roasted bananas over secret fires while humans ate their food raw. When the demigod Māui seized the bird and demanded its secret, it sent him rubbing taro stalks and ti leaves until it was forced to reveal the true fire-drill of rubbing dry sticks together. Furious at the bird's tricks, Māui scorched its forehead, and the mudhen still wears the red mark on its head to this day.
appearance: A small, secretive waterbird, dark-bodied with a bright red plate on its forehead. In Hawaiian tradition the ʻalae ʻula — the endemic moorhen Gallinula galeata sandvicensis — bears the burn Māui left as his punishment.
behavior: Wary and deceptive, the fire-birds lit their fires only when the fishermen were at sea and scratched the coals out whenever anyone returned. In some versions Hina told her son to catch the littlest of the flock, and each lie the bird told about the secret of fire made Māui angrier. Once seized, the bird surrendered fire to humanity on condition its life was spared.
habitat: Coastal marshes and wetlands across the islands
cultural_significance: The bird explains both the origin of the fire-drill and the red forehead of the ʻalae ʻula, a moorhen still honored in Hawaiian tradition as a kinolau (body form) of the goddess Hina.
summary: The ʻalae ʻula fire-bird whose secret of fire-making Maui forced from it, leaving the red burn on its head
fun_fact: In the Hawaiian version fire was not carried away at all — the bird showed that it lives hidden in trees and must be coaxed out by rubbing dry sticks together.
seo_description: The mudhen that kept fire from humanity in the Polynesian origin-of-fire myth, until Maui forced it to reveal the secret of fire-making.
source: Hawaiian origin-of-fire legend — Fornander's Hawaiian Antiquities; M. Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (1940), chs. on Maui; W.D. Westervelt, Legends of Maui; ʻAlae as Hina's kinolau, Ulukau/Kumulipo commentary

name: Hina
description: Hina is the great female deity of Polynesia, known across the Pacific as the moon goddess and as the mother of the demigod Māui. Under the names Hina, Sina, and Ina she rules the moon, the making of tapa cloth, and the sea; the Hawaiian word mahina ('moon') is derived from her name.
appearance: The 'woman in the moon' who beats out tapa — the white, gleaming clouds — with her mallet. In several islands her tapa board, mallet, and calabash are clearly visible in the moon-spots.
behavior: Hina works through the phases of the moon under the names Hinatea ('Fair Hina') and Hinauri ('Dark Hina'). As the mother of Māui she set him great tasks — snaring the sun, lifting the sky, fishing up islands — and, weary of earthly restrictions, finally stepped into the moon, from which she watches over travelers by night.
habitat: The moon and the night sky
weaknesses: the tapu restrictions that drove her away
cultural_significance: One of the most widespread figures in Oceanic religion — attested from Hawaii to Tonga, Samoa, the Society Islands, New Zealand, and Rapa Nui — Hina binds the myths of the far-flung Polynesian groups into a single genealogical family.
summary: The ever-present moon goddess and mother of Maui, known as Hina, Sina, and Ina across all of Polynesia
fun_fact: In the Tahitian tradition Hina stepped into the moon from Motu-tapu on Raiatea, and in Samoa her counterpart Sina is the heroine of the legend of Sina and the Eel that was turned into a coconut tree.
seo_description: Hina, the moon goddess and mother of Maui worshiped as Hina, Sina, and Ina across Polynesia.
source: W.D. Westervelt, Legends of Maui (ch. 'Hina, the Woman in the Moon'); M. Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (1940) ch. 15 'Hina Myths'; W. Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829, Society Islands)

name: Ta'aroa
description: Ta'aroa is the supreme creator god of Tahitian tradition, who existed alone within a cosmic shell and emerged to create the world. In the account recorded by William Ellis, Ta'aroa embraced a rock — the imagined foundation of all things — which brought forth the earth and the sea, and he ordered his son the Sky-producer to call into being the heavens, sun, moon, and stars, and every living thing.
appearance: Formless and original — 'the foundation of all existence', a god of whom the cosmos itself is the body. Shown as a primal figure within his shell, father of all the gods.
behavior: Creator of the universe who set his son to command the sky and sea, and then the ancestor of the gods themselves. When he wished to make mankind, he took the form of the man Ti'i and wooed Hina, and their offspring became the human race.
habitat: The cosmos before the world — space and the primordial deep
weaknesses: the silence and darkness of his solitude
cultural_significance: By the era of the great marae cults Ta'aroa stood at the head of the Tahitian pantheon as supreme deity, and in Tahiti his name was even transferred to the Christian 'God' — a status documented by both Ellis and Teuira Henry.
summary: The supreme creator god of Tahiti who broke his shell to make the world and bred the gods from his rock
fun_fact: Scholars identify Ta'aroa with the sea-god Tangaroa/Tagaloa of the Marquesas and Cook Islands — the same name that became Kanaloa in Hawaiʻi.
seo_description: Ta'aroa, the supreme creator god of Tahitian mythology who emerged from a cosmic shell to make sky, sea, and all life.
source: W. Ellis, Polynesian Researches (1829/1853) — 'Taaroa supreme deity' and the creation tradition; T. Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928); R.W. Williamson, Religious and Cosmic Beliefs of Central Polynesia

name: Rata
description: Rata is the voyager hero of the Society Islands, whose cycle is one of the most widely told oral tales of the Pacific. When his royal father Vahi-e-roa was killed — swallowed by the great clam Pua Tu Tahi in the Tahitian version — Rata felled a sacred tree to build his canoe, only to find it standing whole each morning. He hid and captured the elf-god To'a-hiti and his band who were restoring the tree, and they became his friends and built him a magic canoe in a single night.
appearance: A young warrior chief of Tahiti, shown with the enchanted spear Tevao-roa-ia-Rata at the bow of his spirit-built canoe Va'a-i-ama.
behavior: Determined and dutiful, he sets out to redeem his family's honor: he sails to the vanished land Hiti-marama, cuts open the demon clam to free his parents' bones, and slays the demon bird Matutu-ta'ota'o that swallowed his father's head. After his triumph he sails off into the unknown, and sailors long believed they saw his phantom canoe on the horizon.
habitat: The islands and open ocean of Polynesia, from Tahiti to the Tuamotus
strengths: the magic canoe built by forest elves
cultural_significance: Rata's story is attested from Tonga, Samoa, Tuvalu, the Society and Tuamotu islands, Mangareva, New Zealand, and Hawaiʻi, and its tree-restoring incantation survives in near-identical form across these languages — a living proof of the unity of Polynesian oral literature.
summary: The Society Islands voyager hero who won a spirit-built canoe and avenged his father against a demon clam and demon birds
fun_fact: The incantation Rata overheard — 'fly the leaves, adhere the chips, stand the tree!' — has been reconstructed as a Proto-Polynesian text, one of the oldest recoverable oral compositions of Oceania (Kozmín, JPS 2010).
seo_description: Rata, the culture hero of the Society Islands who built a magic canoe with the forest elves and avenged his father.
source: T. Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928) 468–512; G. Grey, Polynesian Mythology (Māori version); S. Savage, 'The Rarotongan Version of the Story of Rata', JPS 19 (1910); A.V. Kozmín, 'The Tree of Rata: Towards a Reconstruction of a Proto-Polynesian Text', JPS 119 (2010)

name: Atea
description: Atea ('Light', 'The Expanse') is the Marquesan sky deity who, separating himself from Tanaoa the god of Darkness and Silence, drove the dark back and created space for the world. He took the dawn goddess Atanua as his wife, and from their union descended the host of Marquesan gods and, through them, the first humans.
appearance: The bright expanse of the sky itself — a vast luminous being who pushed the primeval dark away from the heavens and the earth.
behavior: A primordial begetter: from his struggle with Darkness came Dawn, and from his marriage to Atanua came the sky-gods and the first men. In Marquesan genealogies he stands as the ultimate ancestor of the chiefs, and of the first man Tiki or Tu-mea.
habitat: The heavens and the space between sky and earth
cultural_significance: In the Marquesas the separation of Atea and Atanua from Tanaoa is the central cosmogonic event, and nineteenth-century genealogies carried the island chiefs back ninety generations to these two deities — a fact recorded by both Handy and Te Rangi Hīroa.
summary: The Marquesan sky god who parted the primal darkness and fathered the gods with the dawn goddess Atanua
fun_fact: Atea is the Marquesan and Tuamotuan form of the great sky-father of Polynesia — Vatea in the Cook Islands and Wakea in Hawaiʻi, where he married the earth goddess Papa.
seo_description: Atea, the light-deity of the Marquesas who separated the heavens from the dark and became ancestor of gods and chiefs.
source: E.S.C. Handy, Marquesan Legends (1930) and The Native Culture in the Marquesas (1923); R.W. Williamson, Religious and Cosmic Beliefs of Central Polynesia; P. Buck (Te Rangi Hīroa), traditional Marquesan genealogies via Hokuleʻa archival project

name: Ti'iti'i
description: Ti'iti'i is the Samoan culture hero who won fire for his people in the western-Polynesian version of the great origin-of-fire cycle. Following his father Talanga into the subterranean land of the earthquake god Mafui'e, Ti'iti'i demanded fire outright, wrestled with the god, and broke off one of his arms; to save the other, Mafui'e revealed that fire is concealed in trees and is drawn out by rubbing dry wood together.
appearance: A bold youth — the Samoan counterpart of Māui and of 'Ti'iti'i-ki'i-ki'i', the littlest of the divine brothers across the Pacific.
behavior: Daring and impertinent: he tricked his way through the rock that guarded the underworld, talked back to a god who 'eats people', and when Mafui'e blew out the family's oven he went straight back to demand answers. When the god attacked, Ti'iti'i wrestled him down and spared his remaining arm only on the promise of fire.
habitat: Samoa and the subterranean land of perpetual fire below the islands
cultural_significance: Samoans credited Ti'iti'i not only with cooked food but with the gentleness of their earthquakes — because Mafui'e needs his single remaining arm to 'hold Samoa straight and level', a one-armed god can never shake the islands too hard.
summary: The Samoan hero who stole fire from the earthquake god Mafui'e and limited Samoa's earthquakes to a single arm
fun_fact: In Samoa a common saying was: 'Thanks to Ti'iti'i that Mafui'e has only one arm — if he had two, what a shake he would give!'
seo_description: Ti'iti'i, the Samoan culture hero who wrestled fire from the earthquake god Mafui'e in the origin-of-fire myth.
source: G. Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before (1884) ch. XIX 'The Origin of Fire and Other Stories'; O. Steubel, Tala o le Vavau: Myths and Legends of Samoa (Brother Herman trans., 1967); W.D. Westervelt, Legends of Maui (1910)
